verdict: Caution on Davangere rice milling: lend only to mills with proven multi-district paddy sourcing and disclosed stock, against collateral and monthly stock statements; avoid single-district, single-season borrowers until Bhadra water and paddy arrivals normalise.
title: Davangere Rice Milling & Export: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A rice mill buys paddy, dries and de-husks it, and sells rice, bran and husk. **Cash is made in the spread between paddy cost and rice price, not in milling fees.** Paddy is the dominant cost; collect from customer the exact paddy-to-rice conversion and by-product realisation for each proposal. Capex is modest (driers, sortex, boiler) but husk-based power and by-product processing are where integrated mills earn extra margin [11]. ## What has broken now
**Paddy arrivals have plunged and mills are running short of raw material** — a national report counts 2,400 rice mills crippled by drought [1]. Locally, Davangere growers are split on Bhadra water timing across around 63,800 hectares, with only around 9,200 hectares transplanted so far, and officials expect a 20% yield decline even if water is released now [2]. So when a proposal lands, check the mill's paddy sourcing map; if it buys only from Davangere, ask where the November-to-January paddy comes from. Note the 2019 local report on mills struggling through drought is old [3] — treat it as history, not current fact. ## Where the growth is
**Peer results show the money is in branded domestic rice and organised exports, not commodity milling.** KRBL posted its strongest-ever quarterly profitability with PAT of Rs. 261 crores and EBITDA margin of 23.8%, up from 13.9% [7]; its domestic revenue grew 22% year-on-year in Q4 FY2026 [4]. Amir Chand Jagdish Kumar's net profit rose 94% to ₹366.27 million on revenue of ₹6,646.74 million [6]. An ICRA note expects 6-8% revenue growth in FY2026 on export pick-up and tier-1/tier-2 domestic demand [8]. Karnataka's GST collections grew 11.1% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1% [D] — a real local demand tailwind. Pursue mills with a brand, a by-product line and export orders; avoid pure custom-milling units with no stock ownership. ## How to grow safely
**Structure against stock, not against hope.** Sanction as a cash-credit limit against pledged paddy and rice stock with a drawing power recalculated monthly, plus a term loan only for sortex/drier assets. Take monthly stock statements, godown inspection reports and paddy purchase bills; take quarterly buyer-wise receivable ageing. Because export receivables carry currency risk [9], insist on hedging or a rupee-denominated book. Note India-wide bank credit grew 26.3% YoY against output of 5.1% [D] — money is chasing this sector faster than it produces, so price for that. ## Early-warning signs
- **Paddy arrival volumes at the mill gate (weekly):** two consecutive weeks below plan -> freeze fresh disbursement and inspect stock. - **Stock statement vs godown physical (monthly):** shortfall above 10% -> stop drawing power and seek explanation in writing. - **Receivable days (monthly):** rising beyond the sanctioned cycle -> shift buyer to LC or cash. - **Bhadra release and transplant acreage (seasonal):** no release by November -> reclassify the borrower's next-season viability. - **Electricity consumption at the mill (monthly):** falling sharply -> check whether the mill has actually stopped running.
